source: Kazemi et al. (2022) LAMBADA: Backward Chaining for Automated Reasoning in Natural Language
finding: Backward chaining (goal to premises, one sub-goal per model call) beats forward chaining and plain chain of thought on proof-style tasks, and needs far fewer model calls as proof depth grows. This is the closest direct forward-versus-backward test for LLMs, but it is logic, not STRIPS planning.
numbers: PaLM 540B. ProofWriter-PUD Depth-5: 44% relative gain over CoT and 56% over Selection-Inference (forward). PrOntoQA Depth-5: 37% over CoT, 113% over SI. ParaRules: 43% over CoT. Calls per example: LAMBADA used 3.8x fewer than SI at Depth-1 and 11.8x fewer at Depth-5.
limits: Logical entailment with rules and facts, not actions with state change. Few-shot PaLM 540B only. No token-matched comparison with long reasoning.
agent_relevance: Supports O5 as a search-space argument: working backward prunes branches that forward chaining explores. Does not show it for state-changing planning (Gap 1 stays open for STRIPS).

source: Kazemi et al. (2022) LAMBADA, backward CoT ablation
finding: Simply writing the chain of thought in backward order does not give the gain. Backward CoT had label accuracy similar to forward CoT but clearly worse proof accuracy. The gain came from the modular loop (rule selection, goal decomposition, fact check, sign agreement), not from direction alone.
numbers: ProofWriter Depth-5: backward CoT label accuracy comparable to forward CoT (better on PD, worse on PUD); proof accuracy substantially lower than forward CoT. Module analysis: rule selection is the weakest module, then goal decomposition; fact check 0.94 with one fact allowed, near perfect with two.
quote: a modular formulation ... is key to successful logical reasoning and simply providing CoT in the backward direction does not suffice
limits: Same dataset and model limits as d01.
agent_relevance: Do not implement O5 as 'think backwards in prose'. It needs explicit sub-goal decomposition with a check at each step.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Reverse Thinking Makes LLMs Stronger Reasoners (RevThink)
finding: Training a student on forward reasoning plus a backward question and backward reasoning raises accuracy on 12 datasets (commonsense, math, logic). A training method, not a scaffold; no planning task.
numbers: Average +13.53% over student zero-shot and +6.84% over the strongest knowledge-distillation baseline across 12 datasets.
limits: Abstract and intro read; training, not an inference scaffold; no planning domain. Gains tied to fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Weak indirect support that backward views help check answers. No evidence for goal regression in planning.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) On the self-verification limitations of LLMs on reasoning and planning tasks, Table 1
finding: Loops with a sound verifier give large gains; an LLM verifier gives little or negative gain. 100 instances per domain, up to 15 rounds.
numbers: Blocksworld: standard 40%, LLM+LLM binary feedback 55%, LLM+sound binary 60%, first-error 87%, all-errors 83%. Sampling with verifier and no critique: k=15 68%, k=25 72%. Self-consistency k=15 42%. Mystery BW: 4 / 0 / 10 / 8 / 6, sampling 9% (k=15) and 14% (k=25). Game of 24: 5 / 3 / 36 / 38; sampling 28% and 42%. Graph colouring: 16 / 2 / 38 / 37 / 34; sampling 40% and 44%.
limits: One lab, GPT-4 era model, 100 instances per domain (about +/-10 points at 95%).
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 4: part of the gain is just more samples checked by a sound verifier. In Blocksworld the first-error message adds 19 points over blind resampling at k=15 (87 vs 68), so precondition-level feedback is worth something; on Mystery BW and graph colouring it is not clearly better.

source: Stechly et al. (2024) self-verification, Table 2 LLM verifier error rates
finding: The LLM as plan verifier makes moderate errors in Blocksworld and extreme false negatives in Mystery Blocksworld. The critic often hallucinated whether a precondition holds.
numbers: Blocksworld accuracy 72.4% (362/500), false positive 6.5% (25/382), false negative 15.48% (24/155). Mystery BW 71.8% (359/500), FP 18.55% (64/345), FN 97.09% (100/103). Game of 24 accuracy 87.0%, FP 10.4%, FN 20.7%.
quote: the critiquing LLM often hallucinates whether action preconditions are met or not
limits: Plan-only input; no variant where the critic sees a precondition trace. Graph colouring row garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open for a trace-reading critic. This is a base rate for plan-only critics (FP 6.5-18.6%, FN 15-97%). Study 2310.08118 reported 84.45% false pass on invalid plans in a differently built set, so rates depend on how invalid plans are made.

source: Stechly et al. (2024) self-verification, loop dynamics and ablation
finding: With an LLM verifier, performance falls as backprompts increase. With a sound verifier it rises monotonically to an asymptote. Dropping critique content and just resampling keeps most of the gain, so the LLM acts mainly as an idea generator.
numbers: Sampling prompts do not grow with round number, so token cost is described as quadratically lower than cumulative backprompts. Self-consistency over 15 samples: 42% on Blocksworld vs 40% standard.
quote: our performance increases seem to stem in large part just from having enough guesses and a sound verifier
limits: Authors' interpretation; one lab; marginal gain per round only shown as a curve (Figure 2), not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: cap rounds, prefer fresh resampling plus a short first-error message over a growing history. Per-round marginal gain not measured numerically; stays open.

source: Valmeekam, Stechly, Kambhampati (2024) LLMs still can't plan; can LRMs? Table 3 and text
finding: o1-preview rarely says a goal is unreachable, and sometimes wrongly calls a solvable one unreachable. Unsolvable goals were made by adding one on(x,y) conjunct to 100 three-to-five block instances, with full PDDL given.
numbers: Blocksworld: 27% correctly flagged, 19% empty plan marker (counted wrong), 54% full impossible plan. Randomized Mystery BW: 16% flagged, 5% empty plan, 79% full plan; 11.5% of solvable instances wrongly called impossible (600 solvable).
limits: One model (o1-preview), one way of making instances unsolvable, 100 instances; no test of a 'prove a plan exists' step.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no evidence for or against an explicit existence-proof step. Put unsolvable items in the test set and let code do a reachability check.

source: Opus and Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking
finding: A comment arguing the reported collapse of reasoning models is mostly an evaluation artefact: output token limits, impossible River Crossing instances, and a grader that scores abbreviation as failure. Preliminary: asking for a function instead of a move list restores high accuracy.
numbers: River Crossing N>=6 with boat capacity 3 is unsolvable (cited result) yet scored as failure. Tower of Hanoi N=15 asked as a Lua function: very high accuracy for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3 and Gemini 2.5, under 5,000 tokens. Estimate used: 10 tokens per move.
limits: Preliminary tests, no sample size reported, short comment; an earlier version had an arithmetic error that the authors corrected.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: format and token budgets can fake a length cliff. Test the cliff with output form held fixed and unsolvable items removed.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking (v3, Nov 2025), FAQ on rebuttals
finding: The authors answer critics: temperature zero does not cause the collapse, River Crossing N>=6 was a flaw (they now focus on N<6), and collapse starts as early as N=3 (11 moves) in River Crossing, far below token limits.
numbers: Budget 64k tokens for Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking and DeepSeek-R1. Blocks World, R1: collapse at N=4 at temperature 0, but sampling delays it to N=30. Tower of Hanoi: failure around move 40 for N=8 (255 moves) and around move 100 for N=10, versus River Crossing failing within 4 correct moves at N=3. Giving the Hanoi algorithm did not raise accuracy.
limits: Controlled puzzles, not PDDL; authors' own rebuttal; the Blocks World collapse point moves 7x with sampling, so a single threshold is fragile.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: 2025-era reasoning models still show a size cliff but its location depends on sampling and puzzle. Report the cliff location with a confidence range.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through The Lens of Efficiency, method and results
finding: An LLM-written successor function and goal test, with search run by plain code, solved all tasks tested, but only after human feedback on corner cases. The paper says passing a test set does not prove the code complete.
numbers: GPT-4 chat, 5 repeats. Game of 24: 1.2 interactions for successor, 1 for goal test; 1362 instances, 1361 solvable solved, the 1 unsolvable reported, 1.92-6.83 s total. Mini crosswords: 2.4 interactions for successor, 1.4 for goal test; 20/20 solved by all 5 variants, 5.5-346 s total (10 candidate answers per clue assumed).
limits: Exact error messages came from a human; 'valid' means valid to a developer who understands the problem. No measured rate of code that passes tests yet is wrong. Crossword setup simplified.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: trust needs an independent test set and, for planning, a comparison against a validator. No study measured silent-error rate; Oswald's 25% equivalence is the only proxy and is for PDDL.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2022) PlanBench, Appendix A.3 obfuscation experiments
finding: Misleading names and random strings both break GPT-4. Randomized names were slightly worse than deceptive ones. Pattern matching on familiar tokens drives the base score, but lost commonsense cues are not separated from memorisation.
numbers: Mystery Blocksworld: deceptive 26/600 (4.3%) GPT-4, 14/600 (0.23%) InstructGPT-3; randomized 12/600 (2%) GPT-4, 6/600 (1%) InstructGPT-3.
quote: more likely due to pattern matching rather than reasoning
limits: Authors' reading. No control keeps names familiar but changes the dynamics, so memorisation and cue loss are not separated.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: partly answered. Scaffold test: rename symbols, and separately change dynamics keeping names; a state-tracking scaffold should lose less in the first.

source: Stechly et al. (2024) self-verification, Mystery Blocksworld row of Table 1
finding: With a sound verifier loop, obfuscated Blocksworld barely gains. A verify-only scaffold did not close the Mystery gap for GPT-4 in that paper.
numbers: Mystery Blocksworld: standard 4%, sound first-error 8%, 25-sample resampling 14%; Blocksworld 40% to 87%.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: scaffolds that only verify do not close the obfuscation drop; the generator must track state itself. Rerun with a newer model.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) NATURAL PLAN, Section 4.4 self-correction
finding: Prompting the model to check and fix its own plan lowers Trip Planning accuracy for all models, and stronger models lose more.
numbers: GPT-4 and Gemini 1.5 Pro lose more than GPT-3.5 (exact drops are in a figure, not read numerically).
limits: No external verifier in the loop; per-model drops not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: self-critique alone is harmful on constraint tasks. Keep external or code checks.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) NATURAL PLAN, main results table
finding: Frontier models of 2024 were poor on natural-language planning with constraints.
numbers: Trip Planning: GPT-3.5 7.3%, GPT-4 31.1%, GPT-4o 3.7%, Gemini 1.5 Flash 25.6%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 34.8%. Meeting Planning: GPT-4 47%, GPT-4o 45.2%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 39.1%.
limits: The authors attribute GPT-4o's 3.7% partly to misreading the task format, so it mixes planning and format failure.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: baseline for non-PDDL transfer; this paper did not measure critic-engineering cost.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: Proposes an LLM that proposes plans plus a bank of external critics (hard critics for correctness such as VAL, soft critics for style). Critics may be written with LLM help from a domain model, which is where the engineering cost sits.
numbers: Quoted figure: only about 12% of GPT-4 plans are executable and goal-reaching in autonomous mode.
quote: only about 12% of the plans that the best LLM (GPT-4) generates are actually executable without errors and goal-reaching
limits: Position paper by the group whose results it cites; no cost accounting for critics.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: hand-written critics are the norm; nobody measured effort or critic error. Not independent of the benchmark authors.

source: Kazemi et al. (2022) LAMBADA, forward chaining redundancy analysis
finding: Forward chaining with an LLM wastes calls on redundant inferences, which explains much of its cost at depth.
numbers: Selection-Inference's five inferred facts per step: 29% had no redundancy, 7% all five identical, 10% only two unique (pie chart, partly garbled). LAMBADA used 11.8x fewer calls at Depth-5.
limits: Pie-chart labels garbled in extraction; percentages approximate.
agent_relevance: Backward search keeps branching small. Gap 1 stays open: needs a STRIPS version.
